name: Sugar Busters

lead: Sugar Busters! is a diet plan from a 1995 self-published book by H. Leighton Steward, Sam Andrews, Morrison Bethea and Luis Balart. It asks followers to avoid refined sugar, white flour and white rice, plus naturally occurring high-glycemic carbohydrates such as potatoes and carrots.

The appearance payoff is via body composition: people use it to lose body fat and look leaner. Published analyses find its weight-loss results comparable to other popular diets and its glycemic load much lower than low-fat plans.

paras: Followers swap refined carbohydrates for lower-glycemic foods, with menus and meal patterns laid out in the book. It is a general eating pattern rather than a time-limited program and is sometimes combined with ordinary exercise.

Published reviews classify it among popular low-carbohydrate-leaning diets and say these plans have little patient-oriented outcome data compared with the Mediterranean diet. One computer analysis estimated that sugar-restricted diets would lower cholesterol and long-term heart-disease risk, while noting lower-fat, higher-fiber diets did so more. People with diabetes or other conditions are generally advised by clinicians to discuss any diet change with their doctor.

angle.text: Followers aim for fat loss through reduced refined carbohydrate intake. Surveys of low-carbohydrate-style diets report mean weight loss of about 18 pounds among current users [5].

lead: Sugar Busters! is a diet plan from a book of the same name, first self-published in 1995 by H. Leighton Steward, Sam S. Andrews, Morrison C. Bethea and Luis A. Balart. It began as a local hit in New Orleans and reached number one on the New York Times bestseller list in June 2001 [1].

The plan centers on cutting refined carbohydrates such as refined sugar, white flour and white rice, and also high-glycemic natural carbohydrates such as potatoes and carrots [1]. People use it to reduce body fat and look leaner; a diet low in sugar is also followed by those who link sugar to skin and energy changes.

Research on it consists of comparative analyses rather than trials of the book's own plan: the American Family Physician review lists it among popular diets with data showing weight loss without increasing disease outcomes [2], a glycemic-index analysis found its median daily glycemic load was less than half that of low-fat plans [3], and a computer analysis compared it with seven other diets [4].
infobox: Avoid refined sugar and high-glycemic carbohydrates

paras: The book, first self-published in 1995 and issued nationally by Ballantine, recommends excluding refined sugar, white flour and white rice and also naturally occurring carbohydrates with a high glycemic index [1]. An updated edition appeared in 2003 [1].

No trial of the Sugar Busters plan alone is among the studies cited here; the research compares it with other diets. A review in American Family Physician said the Atkins, Zone, Sugar Busters and South Beach diets have data showing weight loss without increasing disease-oriented outcomes, but little evidence on patient-oriented benefits, in contrast with the Mediterranean diet [2].

A glycemic analysis of sample menus found median daily glycemic loads of 34 for South Beach and 48 for Sugar Busters, against 113 for the Ornish plan and 104 for EatRight [3]. A computer analysis of eight popular diets estimated that sugar-restricted diets would lower serum cholesterol and long-term coronary risk, though higher-carbohydrate, higher-fiber, lower-fat diets would do so most [4].

A 2002 US telephone survey of 9,300 adults found 12.5% had ever used a low-carbohydrate, high-protein diet, a group that included Sugar Busters; current users reported mean weight loss of 18.3 pounds [5].

Encyclopedic summaries classify Sugar Busters as a fad diet and report its results as comparable to other low-calorie diets [1]. Forum members on T Nation mention it in the context of carbohydrate control, with some describing it as useful for understanding glycemic values and others grouping it with other popular diets [6].
